content: Meclofenamate, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), may increase the risk of heart attack or stroke compared to individuals who do not take NSAIDs. These cardiovascular events can occur without warning and may result in death. The risk is higher for those who use NSAIDs for extended periods. Inform your doctor if you or your family have a history of heart disease, heart attack, or stroke, if you smoke, or if you have high cholesterol, high blood pressure, or diabetes. Seek emergency medical attention immediately if you experience chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side of the body, or slurred speech. Do not take meclofenamate before or after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. NSAIDs, including meclofenamate, can cause ulcers, bleeding, or perforations in the stomach or intestines, which may occur at any time during treatment, often without warning, and can be fatal. The risk is higher for long-term NSAID users, older adults, those in poor health, or individuals who consume large amounts of alcohol while taking the medication. Inform your doctor if you are taking anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), aspirin, other NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen), or oral steroids (e.g., dexamethasone, prednisone). Also, disclose if you have a history of ulcers, gastrointestinal bleeding, or other bleeding disorders. Stop taking meclofenamate and contact your doctor if you experience stomach pain, heartburn, vomiting blood or material resembling coffee grounds, blood in the stool, or black, tarry stools. Regularly attend all medical and laboratory appointments, as your doctor will monitor your symptoms and may order tests to evaluate your response to the medication. Communicate openly with your doctor about how you feel to ensure the appropriate dosage is prescribed to minimize the risk of serious side effects. Your doctor or pharmacist will provide a Medication Guide when you start treatment and with each prescription refill. Read this information carefully and ask any questions you may have. You can also access the Medication Guide on the FDA website. Meclofenamate is prescribed to relieve pain, tenderness, swelling, and stiffness associated with osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. It is also used for mild to moderate pain, including menstrual pain, and to reduce heavy menstrual bleeding. It belongs to the NSAID class of medications and works by inhibiting the production of substances in the body that cause pain, fever, and inflammation. Meclofenamate is available as an oral capsule and is typically taken three to four times daily for arthritis, three times daily for heavy menstrual bleeding, or every 4-6 hours as needed for pain. It can be taken with food or milk to prevent stomach upset. If taken regularly, maintain a consistent schedule. Follow your prescription instructions carefully and do not alter the dosage without consulting your doctor. If you are using meclofenamate for heavy menstrual bleeding, your bleeding should decrease during treatment. Contact your doctor if it does not improve or if you experience spotting or bleeding between periods. For arthritis, symptom improvement may begin within a few days, but full benefits may take 2-3 weeks or longer. Meclofenamate is also used to treat ankylosing spondylitis, gouty arthritis, and psoriatic arthritis. Discuss the risks of using this medication with your doctor. It may also be prescribed for other conditions; consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking meclofenamate, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to it, aspirin, other NSAIDs, or any inactive ingredients in the capsules. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Your doctor may need to adjust your medications or monitor you for side effects. Disclose any history of conditions mentioned in the warning section, asthma (especially with nasal polyps), swelling in extremities, or liver or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking meclofenamate, contact your doctor immediately. Notify your healthcare provider if you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless it is close to the next scheduled dose. Do not double the dose to compensate for a missed one. Meclofenamate may cause side effects. Report persistent or severe symptoms such as diarrhea, constipation, gas, mouth sores, headache, or ringing in the ears to your doctor. Serious side effects require immediate medical attention and discontinuation of the medication. These include blurred vision, unexplained weight gain, fever, blisters, rash, itching, hives, swelling of the face or extremities, hoarseness, difficulty breathing or swallowing, yellowing of the skin or eyes, fatigue, unusual bleeding or bruising, lack of energy, stomach pain, flu-like symptoms, pale skin, rapid heartbeat, discolored or bloody urine, back pain, or painful urination. If you experience any unusual problems while taking meclofenamate, contact your doctor. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store meclofenamate in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Dispose of expired or unneeded medication properly, consulting your pharmacist for guidance. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include irrational behavior, agitation, seizures, or reduced urination. Do not share this medication with others. Consult your pharmacist with any questions about refilling your prescription.
